en: The Questions of Milinda, Chapter on Investigation, 6. The Question on the Knower of All "Venerable sir," said King Milinda, "is there anyone who knows all? "There is, great king," replied the Venerable Nāgasena. "But who is it, venerable sir? "The Tathāgata, great king, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. "But, venerable sir, how does the Tathāgata know all? Does he know all by means of the eye of flesh? "No, great king. "Does he know all by means of the divine eye? "No, great king. "Does he know all by means of the eye of wisdom? "No, great king. "Does he know all by means of the eye of Dhamma? "No, great king. "Does he know all by means of the eye of liberation? "No, great king. "Then, venerable sir, does the Tathāgata know nothing at all? "No, great king. It is not that the Tathāgata knows nothing at all. But, great king, the Tathāgata knows all by means of the knowledge of omniscience. "But, venerable sir, what is this knowledge of omniscience? "It is, great king, that knowledge which is unobstructed regarding the past, the future, and the present; which is unimpeded regarding the infinite variety of phenomena; which is the knowledge of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. "But, venerable sir, is this knowledge of omniscience something that can be pointed out like a pillar or a wall? "No, great king. "Then, venerable sir, is it something that can be seen with the eye? "No, great king. "Is it something that can be heard with the ear? "No, great king. "Is it something that can be smelled with the nose? "No, great king. "Is it something that can be tasted with the tongue? "No, great king. "Is it something that can be felt with the body? "No, great king. "Is it something that can be known with the mind? "No, great king. "Then, venerable sir, is it something that does not exist at all? "No, great king. It is not that it does not exist at all. But, great king, this knowledge of omniscience is something that cannot be pointed out, nor seen, nor heard, nor smelled, nor tasted, nor felt, nor known by the mind. Yet, great king, it exists. "Just as, great king, the element of space cannot be pointed out, nor seen, nor heard, nor smelled, nor tasted, nor felt, nor known by the mind, yet it exists; even so, great king, this knowledge of omniscience cannot be pointed out... yet it exists. "But, venerable sir, if this knowledge of omniscience cannot be pointed out... yet it exists, then how can one say, 'The Tathāgata knows all'? "Great king, suppose there were a man who had never before seen the ocean, and he asked a man who had lived by the sea for many years, 'What is the ocean like? And the man who had lived by the sea replied, 'It is deep, vast, and immeasurable. Now, great king, would that man who had never seen the ocean believe him when he said, 'It is deep, vast, and immeasurable'? "Yes, venerable sir, he would believe him. "And why so? "Because the man who had lived by the sea is trustworthy and reliable. "In the same way, great king, the Tathāgata is trustworthy and reliable. Therefore, when he says, 'I know all,' one should believe him. "But, venerable sir, how does the Tathāgata know all? "Great king, the Tathāgata knows all by means of the knowledge of omniscience, which is unobstructed and unimpeded regarding the past, the future, and the present. "But, venerable sir, if the Tathāgata knows all by means of the knowledge of omniscience, then is he not omniscient at every single moment? "No, great king. It is not that he is omniscient at every single moment. But, great king, the Tathāgata knows all by means of the knowledge of omniscience, which is unobstructed and unimpeded. "Just as, great king, a king who possesses a precious gem that grants all wishes does not have to think, 'I shall now produce this wish, or I shall now produce that wish,' but rather, whenever he desires anything, that wish is fulfilled by the power of the gem; even so, great king, the Tathāgata does not have to think, 'I shall now know this, or I shall now know that,' but rather, whenever he desires to know anything, that knowledge arises by the power of the knowledge of omniscience.

"But, venerable sir, if the Tathāgata knows all by means of the knowledge of omniscience, then does he not know everything simultaneously? "No, great king. It is not that he knows everything simultaneously. But, great king, the Tathāgata knows all by means of the knowledge of omniscience, which is unobstructed and unimpeded. "Just as, great king, a man who possesses a mirror does not have to think, 'I shall now see my reflection, or I shall now see my face,' but rather, whenever he looks into the mirror, he sees his reflection and his face; even so, great king, the Tathāgata does not have to think, 'I shall now know this, or I shall now know that,' but rather, whenever he desires to know anything, that knowledge arises by the power of the knowledge of omniscience. "But, venerable sir, if the Tathāgata knows all by means of the knowledge of omniscience, then is he not a knower of all things? "Yes, great king, the Tathāgata is a knower of all things. "But, venerable sir, if he is a knower of all things, then does he not know the minds of others? "Yes, great king, he knows the minds of others. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the minds of others, then does he not know the thoughts of those who are far away? "Yes, great king, he knows them. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the thoughts of those who are far away, then does he not know the secrets of their hearts? "Yes, great king, he knows them. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the secrets of their hearts, then does he not know the intentions of those who are about to die? "Yes, great king, he knows them. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the intentions of those who are about to die, then does he not know the state of their rebirth? "Yes, great king, he knows it. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the state of their rebirth, then does he not know the kamma that leads to that rebirth? "Yes, great king, he knows it. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the kamma that leads to that rebirth, then does he not know the causes and conditions for that kamma? "Yes, great king, he knows them. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the causes and conditions for that kamma, then does he not know the results of that kamma? "Yes, great king, he knows them. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the results of that kamma, then does he not know the future consequences of those results? "Yes, great king, he knows them. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the future consequences of those results, then does he not know the end of suffering? "Yes, great king, he knows it. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the end of suffering, then does he not know the path leading to the end of suffering? "Yes, great king, he knows it. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the path leading to the end of suffering, then does he not know the practice of that path? "Yes, great king, he knows it. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the practice of that path, then does he not know the fruits of that practice? "Yes, great king, he knows them. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the fruits of that practice, then does he not know the attainment of those fruits? "Yes, great king, he knows it. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the attainment of those fruits, then does he not know the cessation of those fruits? "Yes, great king, he knows it. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the cessation of those fruits, then does he not know the transcendence of that cessation? "Yes, great king, he knows it. "But, venerable sir, if he knows the transcendence of that cessation, then does he not know the ultimate goal? "Yes, great king, he knows it. "But, venerable sir, if he knows
The King said:
"Venerable Nāgasena, is an omniscient one (vedagu) found?
"But who, Great King, is this so-called omniscient one?"
“Venerable sir, that living being within who sees forms with the eye, hears sounds with the ear, smells odors with the nose,
tastes flavors with the tongue, touches tangibles with the body, and cognizes mental phenomena with the mind—
just as we here, sitting in this palace, can look out through whichever window we wish;”

“Through this or that window we might look out; through the eastern window we might look out, through the western window we might look out, through the northern window we might look out, and through the southern window we might look out.
In the same way, venerable sir, this inner life-principle looks out through whichever door it wishes to look out.”
The Elder said:
"I shall speak, Great King, of the five doors; listen to it and attend to it well.
If the soul within sees a form with the eye, just as we here, sitting in this palace, [see] through whichever window..."
We would wish to see; through each and every window we would see only forms:

through the eastern window we would see only forms, through the western window we would see only forms, through the northern window we would see only forms, and through the southern window we would see only forms—in this way, within here.
With the eye, one should see only form; with the nose, one should see only form; with the tongue, one should see only form;
with the body, one should see only form; with the mind, one should see only form.

With the ear, one should hear only sound; with the nose, one should hear only sound; with the tongue, one should hear only sound; with the body, one should hear only sound; with the mind, one should hear only sound.

By the eye, only odor is to be smelled; by the ear, only odor is to be smelled; by the tongue, only odor is to be smelled; by the body, only odor is to be smelled; by the mind, only odor is to be smelled.
By the eye, only taste is to be tasted; by the ear, only taste is to be tasted; by the nose, only taste is to be tasted; by the body, only taste is to be tasted;
by the mind, only taste is to be tasted. By the eye, only the tangible is to be touched; by the ear, only the tangible is to be touched; by the nose, only the tangible...
“Is it only the tangible that is to be touched by the body, and only the tangible that is to be touched by the tongue, and only the tangible that is to be touched by the mind?
And is it only the mental object that is to be cognized by the eye, and only the mental object that is to be cognized by the ear, and only the mental object that is to be cognized by the nose,
and only the mental object that is to be cognized by the tongue, and only the mental object that is to be cognized by the body?”
“No indeed, Bhante.
“It is not consistent for you, Great King, that the latter should agree with the former, or the former with the latter.
For instance, Great King, while we are sitting here in this palace and these lattice windows are opened, with a great [light]...”

Just as we see forms very clearly through space when facing outward, so too, when the internal life-principle has opened up the doors of the eye, one should see forms very clearly through that great space;
when the ears are opened… when the nose is opened… when the tongue is opened… when the body is opened, one should see very clearly through the great space.
“Sound is to be heard, smell is to be smelled, taste is to be tasted, and touch is to be touched?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
“Then, Great King, it does not logically follow for you that the latter corresponds to the former, nor that the former corresponds to the latter.”
"Or again, Great King, suppose this Dinna were to go out and stand outside the gateway;
would you know, Great King, 'This Dinna has gone out and is standing outside the gateway'?
"Yes, venerable sir, I would know it."
“Or again, great king, suppose this Dinna were to enter inside and stand before you; would you know, great king, ‘This Dinna has entered inside and is standing before me’?
“Yes, venerable sir, I would know.
“In the same way, great king, when a taste is placed upon the tongue, that living being within would know its sourness, or saltiness, or bitterness, or pungency, or astringency, or sweetness.”
“Yes, venerable sir, one would know.
“If those flavors had entered inside, would one know whether they were sour, salty, bitter, pungent, astringent, or sweet?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“It is not logical for you, Great King, that the latter should agree with the former, or the former with the latter.

Suppose, Great King, some man were to have a hundred jars of honey brought, fill a trough with honey, cover a man’s mouth, and throw him into that trough of honey; would that man, Great King, know whether the honey was of good quality?”
“Or is it not accomplished?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“For what reason?”
“Indeed, venerable sir, no honey has entered his mouth.
“It is not consistent for you, Great King, to say the latter in light of the former, or the former in light of the latter.
“I am not capable of conversing with such a debater as yourself.”
“Excellent, venerable sir; please speak for our benefit.
The Elder instructed King Milinda with a discourse connected to the Abhidhamma:
“In this case, Great King, dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; co-nascent with that [consciousness]…”
Contact, feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness, the life-faculty, and attention—thus these phenomena arise by way of condition;
herein no "knower" (vedagu) is found. Dependent on the ear and sounds ... [and so on] ...
dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises; together with that [consciousness], there arise contact, feeling, and perception.
“Volition, one-pointedness, the life-faculty, and attention—in this way these phenomena arise through conditions;
herein no experiencer is found.
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena!”
The sixth question: On the Veda-master.
